name: SST
summary: A TypeScript framework that defines a whole app, from Next.js front end to functions, containers and databases, in one config file and deploys it to your own AWS or Cloudflare account.
intro: An SST app is described in one file, `sst.config.ts`. Instead of listing low-level resources, you create components: `sst.aws.Nextjs` for a front end with its domain, `sst.aws.Function` for a Lambda function, `sst.aws.Service` for an always-on container on ECS and Fargate, plus buckets, Postgres databases, cron jobs, and Cloudflare Workers. Each component creates the underlying resources with sensible defaults, and a `transform` option lets you change any of them. Beyond the built-in AWS and Cloudflare components you can use resources from any of the 150+ Pulumi and Terraform providers, such as Stripe, Vercel or PlanetScale.

Under the hood SST uses Pulumi’s deployment engine with Terraform-based providers. It runs from your machine or CI, keeps its state file locally and backs it up to a bucket in your account, with secrets in the state encrypted by a passphrase stored in SSM. Two features target the inner loop. Linking (`link: [bucket]`) grants a function or site permission to a resource and gives your code typed access to it, as `Resource.MyBucket.name`. `sst dev` deploys the app to a development stage and proxies its Lambda invocations to your laptop, so code changes take effect without a redeploy.

SST is open source under MIT, built by Anomaly Innovations, which also makes opencode, OpenNext and OpenAuth and sells the optional SST Console for logs, issues and automatic deploys. Versions 1 and 2 were built on the AWS CDK and CloudFormation; version 3 (2024) replaced both, and version 4 (February 2026) moved to version 7 of the Pulumi AWS provider. The latest release is 4.17.1, from July 2026.
strengths: High-level components for frameworks like Next.js, Remix, Astro and SvelteKit, so a full-stack app is a few lines of config
Live Lambda development: `sst dev` runs functions locally against real AWS events, with breakpoints and the function’s real IAM permissions
Resource linking replaces hand-written IAM policies and environment variables, with typed SDKs for JS/TS, Python, Go and Rust
No CloudFormation underneath since v3: no stacks, no 500-resource limit per stack, and any Pulumi or Terraform provider
limits: Major versions have meant migrations: v3 dropped CDK constructs, which had to be rewritten, and v4 needs a one-way state refresh on every stage
Built-in components exist only for AWS and Cloudflare; anything else is lower-level provider resources
The config is TypeScript, and the project depends on one small company whose team also works on other products
Another layer between you and the cloud: when a component’s defaults don’t fit, you debug its generated Pulumi resources

story: SST started in 2020 as Serverless Stack, a framework for building serverless apps on AWS that launched publicly in 2021. It was built on the AWS CDK, so its constructs generated CloudFormation templates that AWS then deployed. In June 2022 it renamed itself SST, partly to stop being confused with the Serverless Framework, and moved to sst.dev; v1 had shipped that May and a rewritten v2 followed in February 2023.

After nearly three years on CDK and CloudFormation, the team decided the foundations were the problem. A January 2024 post listed what they kept hitting: CloudFormation runs as a black box on AWS’s side, failed deployments can get stuck rolling back, every stack is limited to 500 resources (a Next.js site alone created around 68), and supporting a non-AWS provider such as Cloudflare would need custom-resource hacks. They began a new engine, code-named Ion, built on Pulumi and Terraform providers.

Ion was released as SST v3 in August 2024, with no CDK, no CloudFormation and support for 150+ providers. SST v4, in February 2026, was a smaller step that moved to the Pulumi AWS provider v7. Meanwhile the company behind it, Anomaly, broadened its work to opencode, an open-source AI coding agent, alongside OpenNext and OpenAuth.

choices.choice: Start on top of the AWS CDK
choices.why: CDK already modelled every AWS resource and deployed through CloudFormation, so a small team could focus on higher-level constructs and live development instead of a deployment engine.

choices.choice: Replace CDK and CloudFormation with Pulumi and Terraform providers
choices.why: CloudFormation’s opaque execution, slow and sometimes stuck rollbacks and 500-resource stack limit kept hurting users, and it couldn’t deploy to providers like Cloudflare without workarounds.

choices.choice: Run Lambda functions on the developer’s machine during development
choices.why: Redeploying a function to test every change is slow. Proxying invocations from AWS to the laptop gives sub-second reloads and real breakpoints while still using real events and permissions.

choices.choice: Link resources instead of wiring permissions by hand
choices.why: Connecting a function to a bucket normally means an IAM policy plus an environment variable with the bucket’s name. One `link` does both and gives the code typed access.

timeline.text: Repository created as Serverless Stack, built on the AWS CDK
SST v1 in May; renamed from Serverless Stack to SST in June
SST v2, a rewrite into a single `sst` package, in February
Team announces Ion in January; released as SST v3 in August
SST v4 moves to the Pulumi AWS provider v7 in February
